_meta: Two variables generated by a known structural model in which Y causes X (Y -> X, with X := 2*Y plus a small fixed perturbation), used to show that correlation cannot reveal the direction of causation -- the same data fits X -> Y and Y -> X equally well, and only an intervention distinguishes them. An analyst who sees a strong correlation between X and Y and concludes 'X drives Y, so change X to move Y' has assumed a direction the data does not contain. For a simple linear relationship the coefficient of determination R-squared is exactly the squared correlation regardless of which variable is regressed on which, so regressing Y on X and regressing X on Y fit the data identically -- the observational data is symmetric in the two variables and says nothing about which is cause and which is effect. The asymmetry that does carry direction is intervention: in the true model Y -> X, setting X externally (an intervention on X) does not change Y, because X is downstream and the edge from Y to X does not run backward, whereas setting Y changes X. So the discriminating experiment is to intervene: if forcing X leaves Y unmoved while forcing Y moves X, the arrow runs Y -> X, the reverse of the naive reading. y_values are the exogenous cause; slope is the true structural coefficient of the Y -> X edge; noise is a small fixed perturbation added to X so the correlation is high but not degenerate. These are the fixture; the correlation, the two regression fits, and the two intervention effects are computed.
